units.note:
# Unit 1: Kinematics

## Overview
This unit introduces **kinematics**, the branch of physics describing motion without considering its causes. You will learn to analyze **displacement**, **velocity**, and **acceleration**, apply **kinematic equations** to solve problems, and interpret **graphs of motion**. Mastery of these concepts is essential for solving AP Physics 1 problems involving linear and projectile motion.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**           | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                         |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Displacement**      | Vector quantity representing change in position, $$\vec{d} = \vec{x}_f - \vec{x}_i$$ | Distinguishes from distance; critical for vector analysis problems. |
| **Velocity**          | Rate of change of displacement; vector $$\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{x}}{dt}$$        | Differentiates speed from velocity; key in interpreting motion graphs.|
| **Acceleration**      | Rate of change of velocity; vector $$\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$$            | Central to understanding changing motion and applying kinematic equations.|
| **Kinematic Equations** | Set of equations relating $$\vec{d}, \vec{v}, \vec{a}, t$$ for constant acceleration | Fundamental tools for solving linear motion problems on the exam.   |
| **Projectile Motion** | Two-dimensional motion under gravity, decomposed into independent horizontal and vertical components | Tests ability to analyze motion in 2D and apply kinematics separately.|
| **Graphical Analysis**| Interpretation of position, velocity, and acceleration vs. time graphs          | Essential for qualitative and quantitative problem solving.          |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start: Define Motion Scenario"] --> B["Identify Known Variables (x_i, v_i, a, t)"]
    B --> C["Choose Appropriate Kinematic Equation"]
    C --> D["Solve for Unknown (x_f, v_f, t)"]
    D --> E["Interpret Results (displacement, velocity, acceleration)"]
    E --> F{"Is Motion 2D (Projectile)? "}
    F -- Yes --> G["Resolve Motion into x and y components"]
    G --> H["Apply 1D Kinematic Equations Separately"]
    H --> I["Combine Results for Final Solution"]
    F -- No --> J["Use 1D Kinematics Directly"]
    J --> I
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| Formula / Rule                      | Description                                          |
|-----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| $$\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{x}}{dt}$$ | Instantaneous velocity as derivative of position     |
| $$\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt}$$ | Instantaneous acceleration as derivative of velocity |
| Constant acceleration kinematics: |                                                      |
| $$v = v_0 + at$$                  | Velocity after time $$t$$                             |
| $$x = x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2$$ | Displacement after time $$t$$                    |
| $$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)$$    | Velocity-displacement relation without time           |
| Projectile motion components:     |                                                      |
| Horizontal: $$x = v_{0x} t$$      | Constant velocity (no horizontal acceleration)        |
| Vertical: $$y = y_0 + v_{0y} t - \frac{1}{2} g t^2$$ | Vertical displacement under gravity $$g$$ |
| Vertical velocity: $$v_y = v_{0y} - g t$$ | Vertical velocity at time $$t$$                      |
| Gravity acceleration: $$g = 9.8 \, m/s^2$$ | Constant downward acceleration near Earth's surface |

## Connections & Comparisons

| Concept 1           | Concept 2           | Similarities                                    | Differences / AP Focus                                      |
|---------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Displacement**     | **Distance**        | Both measure length of motion                   | Displacement is vector (direction matters), distance is scalar (always positive) |
| **Velocity**         | **Speed**           | Both measure how fast an object moves           | Velocity is vector (direction + magnitude), speed is scalar (magnitude only)    |
| **Acceleration**     | **Velocity Change** | Acceleration causes velocity to change          | Acceleration is rate of velocity change; velocity change is the effect         |
| **Horizontal Motion**| **Vertical Motion** | Both use kinematic equations                     | Horizontal velocity constant (no acceleration), vertical velocity affected by gravity |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **displacement** with **distance**; displacement can be zero if start and end points coincide, distance cannot.
- Forgetting to treat **velocity** and **acceleration** as vectors; direction matters, especially in projectile motion.
- Applying kinematic equations assuming constant acceleration when acceleration varies (e.g., air resistance ignored).
- Mixing up horizontal and vertical components in projectile problems; they must be analyzed independently.
- Misinterpreting motion graphs, especially confusing slope and area under curves for position, velocity, and acceleration.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define and distinguish **displacement**, **velocity**, and **acceleration** as vectors.
- [ ] Use and rearrange the **kinematic equations** for constant acceleration.
- [ ] Analyze **projectile motion** by decomposing into horizontal and vertical components.
- [ ] Interpret **position vs. time**, **velocity vs. time**, and **acceleration vs. time** graphs.
- [ ] Solve problems involving motion with **constant acceleration**, including free fall.
- [ ] Recognize and avoid common pitfalls in vector direction and sign conventions.
- [ ] Calculate time, displacement, and velocity for 1D and 2D motion scenarios.
- [ ] Explain the independence of horizontal and vertical motions in projectile motion.

# Unit 2: Force and Translational Dynamics

## Overview
This unit explores **Newton's three laws of motion** and their application to forces acting on objects in translational motion. You will learn to analyze forces such as **friction**, **normal force**, and **tension**, and use **free-body diagrams** to solve problems involving **translational equilibrium**. Mastery of these concepts is essential for solving AP Physics 1 problems involving motion and force interactions.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**           | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                         |
|----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Newton's First Law    | An object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net force. | Foundation for understanding inertia and equilibrium conditions.    |
| Newton's Second Law   | $$\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a}$$ relates net force, mass, and acceleration.        | Central equation for solving dynamics problems on the exam.          |
| Newton's Third Law    | For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.               | Crucial for analyzing force pairs and interaction problems.          |
| Friction             | Force opposing relative motion between surfaces; static and kinetic types.     | Often appears in problems requiring force balance and motion analysis.|
| Normal Force          | Perpendicular contact force exerted by a surface on an object.                 | Key to correctly setting up free-body diagrams and force components. |
| Tension              | Force transmitted through a string, rope, or cable when pulled tight.          | Common in pulley and connected-object problems on the AP exam.       |
| Free-Body Diagrams   | Visual representation of all forces acting on an object.                       | Essential tool for organizing and solving force and motion problems. |
| Translational Equilibrium | Condition where $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$ and acceleration is zero.               | Basis for static and constant velocity scenarios tested on the exam. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Identify the object of interest"] --> B["Draw Free-Body Diagram (FBD)"]
    B --> C["List all forces: gravity, normal, friction, tension, applied"]
    C --> D["Resolve forces into components (if needed)"]
    D --> E["Apply Newton's Second Law: $$\sum F_x = ma_x$$ and $$\sum F_y = ma_y$$"]
    E --> F["Solve for unknowns: acceleration, force magnitudes, tension, etc."]
    F --> G{"Is acceleration zero?"}
    G -- Yes --> H["Translational Equilibrium: $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$"]
    G -- No --> I["Object accelerates: $$\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a}$$"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| Formula / Law                          | Description                                              |
|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| $$\vec{F}_{net} = \sum \vec{F}$$    | Vector sum of all forces acting on an object.            |
| $$\vec{F}_{net} = m \vec{a}$$        | Newton's Second Law relating net force and acceleration. |
| $$f_s \leq \mu_s N$$                 | Maximum static friction force; $$\mu_s$$ is static friction coefficient. |
| $$f_k = \mu_k N$$                    | Kinetic friction force; $$\mu_k$$ is kinetic friction coefficient. |
| $$N = mg \cos \theta$$               | Normal force on an inclined plane at angle $$\theta$$.   |
| $$T$$                               | Tension force in a string or rope (magnitude along the rope). |
| Newton's First Law                   | $$\vec{a} = 0 \Rightarrow \sum \vec{F} = 0$$ (equilibrium). |
| Newton's Third Law                   | $$\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$$ (action-reaction pairs). |

## Connections & Comparisons

| Concept 1          | Concept 2           | Similarities                                    | Differences / AP Focus                                  |
|--------------------|---------------------|------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Static Friction    | Kinetic Friction    | Both oppose relative motion between surfaces.  | Static friction adjusts up to $$\mu_s N$$; kinetic friction is constant $$\mu_k N$$ and acts during motion. |
| Normal Force       | Weight (Gravity)    | Both are forces acting on an object.            | Weight acts downward due to gravity; normal force acts perpendicular to contact surface. |
| Newton's First Law | Newton's Second Law | Both describe motion states and forces.         | First law describes equilibrium (no acceleration); second law quantifies acceleration when net force exists. |
| Tension            | Normal Force        | Both are contact forces transmitted through objects. | Tension acts along a rope/string; normal force acts perpendicular to a surface. |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **static friction** with **kinetic friction**; static friction varies up to a maximum, kinetic friction is constant.
- Forgetting to include all forces in the **free-body diagram**, especially the **normal force** and **friction**.
- Treating **tension** as a separate force rather than a force transmitted through a string or rope.
- Misapplying Newton's Third Law by mixing action-reaction pairs on the **same object** instead of on **different objects**.
- Assuming **translational equilibrium** (zero acceleration) without checking if the net force is zero.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Explain and apply **Newton's three laws** to various physical situations.
- [ ] Draw accurate **free-body diagrams** including all relevant forces.
- [ ] Distinguish between **static** and **kinetic friction** and calculate frictional forces.
- [ ] Calculate **normal force** on flat and inclined surfaces.
- [ ] Analyze **tension** forces in strings and ropes in multi-object systems.
- [ ] Solve problems involving **translational equilibrium** where $$\sum \vec{F} = 0$$.
- [ ] Use Newton’s Second Law $$\sum \vec{F} = m \vec{a}$$ to find acceleration or unknown forces.
- [ ] Identify and correctly apply **action-reaction force pairs** per Newton’s Third Law.

units.note:
# Unit 3: Work, Energy, and Power

## Overview
This unit explores the fundamental concepts of **work**, **energy**, and **power**, focusing on how forces affect the motion and energy of objects. Understanding the **work-energy theorem**, **conservative forces**, and the **conservation of mechanical energy** is crucial for solving problems involving energy transfer and efficiency, which are frequently tested on the AP Physics 1 exam.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**                 | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                           |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Work**                   | The transfer of energy by a force acting over a displacement: $$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$$ | Central to understanding energy changes; appears in problem-solving.  |
| **Kinetic Energy (KE)**    | Energy of motion: $$KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$                                    | Quantifies how motion relates to energy; key for work-energy theorem.  |
| **Potential Energy (PE)**  | Stored energy due to position, e.g., gravitational: $$PE = mgh$$               | Helps analyze energy conservation and forces in systems.              |
| **Work-Energy Theorem**    | Work done equals change in kinetic energy: $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$$     | Connects forces and motion; simplifies dynamics problems.              |
| **Conservative Forces**    | Forces where work done is path-independent (e.g., gravity, spring force)       | Allows use of energy conservation; reduces complexity in calculations.|
| **Nonconservative Forces** | Forces like friction where energy is lost as heat, path-dependent work         | Important for realistic problem setups; affects total mechanical energy.|
| **Conservation of Mechanical Energy** | Total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant if only conservative forces act | Fundamental principle for solving many AP problems without force analysis.|
| **Power**                  | Rate of doing work or transferring energy: $$P = \frac{W}{t} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$$ | Measures how quickly energy is used or transferred; common in real-world contexts.|

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Apply Force ($\vec{F}$) over Displacement ($\vec{d}$)"] --> B["Calculate Work: $W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d}$"]
    B --> C["Determine Change in Kinetic Energy: $\Delta KE$"]
    C --> D["Use Work-Energy Theorem: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE$"]
    D --> E{"Are forces conservative?"}
    E -- Yes --> F["Apply Conservation of Mechanical Energy: $KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f$"]
    E -- No --> G["Account for Nonconservative Work (e.g., friction)"]
    G --> H["Calculate Total Energy Change and Power"]
    F --> H
    H --> I["Calculate Power: $P = \frac{W}{t}$ or $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| Formula / Law                              | Description                                                  |
|-------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| $$W = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{d} = F d \cos \theta$$ | Work done by a constant force over displacement $$d$$ at angle $$\theta$$ |
| $$KE = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$                | Kinetic energy of an object with mass $$m$$ and speed $$v$$  |
| $$PE_{gravity} = m g h$$                   | Gravitational potential energy relative to reference height $$h$$ |
| $$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta KE = KE_f - KE_i$$ | Work-energy theorem connecting net work and kinetic energy change |
| $$E_{\text{mech}} = KE + PE$$              | Total mechanical energy of a system                          |
| $$E_{\text{mech, initial}} = E_{\text{mech, final}}$$ (if conservative forces only) | Conservation of mechanical energy principle                  |
| $$W_{\text{nc}} = \Delta E_{\text{mech}}$$ | Work done by nonconservative forces equals mechanical energy change |
| $$P = \frac{W}{t}$$ or $$P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$$ | Power as rate of work or dot product of force and velocity    |

## Connections & Comparisons

| Concept                     | Conservative Forces                          | Nonconservative Forces                      | Impact on Energy Conservation                  |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| **Definition**              | Work done independent of path                | Work depends on path                         | Determines if mechanical energy is conserved   |
| **Examples**                | Gravity, spring force                         | Friction, air resistance                     | Conservative: $$E_{\text{mech}} = \text{constant}$$; Nonconservative: $$E_{\text{mech}} \downarrow$$ |
| **Work Done**               | $$W = -\Delta PE$$ (negative change in PE)  | Converts mechanical energy to thermal, sound, etc. | Nonconservative work changes total mechanical energy |
| **Energy Accounting**       | Use conservation of mechanical energy        | Must include $$W_{\text{nc}}$$ in energy balance | Nonconservative forces cause energy dissipation |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Forgetting to include the angle $$\theta$$ between force and displacement when calculating work.
- Confusing **work done by a force** with **change in kinetic energy** without applying the work-energy theorem correctly.
- Assuming mechanical energy is conserved when **nonconservative forces** like friction are present.
- Misapplying the formula for **power** by ignoring the vector nature of force and velocity.
- Neglecting to choose a proper reference point for **potential energy** calculations.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define and calculate **work** done by a constant force.
- [ ] Explain and apply the **work-energy theorem** to relate net work and kinetic energy change.
- [ ] Calculate **kinetic** and **potential energy** for various systems.
- [ ] Identify **conservative** vs. **nonconservative forces** and their effects on energy.
- [ ] Use **conservation of mechanical energy** to solve problems without force analysis.
- [ ] Calculate **power** as rate of work or using force and velocity.
- [ ] Analyze energy transformations when **nonconservative forces** act.
- [ ] Avoid common pitfalls related to angles, reference points, and force types in energy problems.

units.note:
# Unit 4: Linear Momentum

## Overview
This unit explores **linear momentum**, a fundamental quantity describing motion, and how it changes through forces and collisions. Understanding the **impulse-momentum theorem**, **conservation of linear momentum**, and the nature of **elastic and inelastic collisions** is essential for solving AP Physics 1 problems involving interacting objects and forces over time.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**                  | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                               |
|-----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Linear Momentum**          | Product of an object's mass and velocity: $$\vec{p} = m \vec{v}$$              | Momentum conservation is a core principle tested in collision problems.    |
| **Impulse**                  | Change in momentum caused by a force applied over time: $$\vec{J} = \vec{F} \Delta t$$ | Connects force and time to changes in motion; key for impulse-momentum problems. |
| **Impulse-Momentum Theorem** | $$\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{p}$$ — Impulse equals change in momentum               | Allows solving for unknown forces, times, or velocities in dynamic scenarios. |
| **Conservation of Momentum** | Total momentum before collision equals total momentum after, if no external forces | Fundamental for analyzing collisions and explosions on the AP exam.          |
| **Elastic Collisions**       | Collisions where kinetic energy and momentum are conserved                      | Requires applying two conservation laws simultaneously; common AP problem type. |
| **Inelastic Collisions**     | Collisions where objects stick or deform; momentum conserved but kinetic energy is not | Tests understanding of energy dissipation and momentum conservation.         |
| **Center of Mass (COM)**     | Weighted average position of mass in a system                                  | Useful for analyzing system motion and collisions in multi-object systems.   |
| **System vs. External Forces** | Distinguishing internal forces (between system parts) and external forces       | Critical for correctly applying conservation laws on the AP exam.            |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start: Two Objects Approach"] --> B["Identify System and External Forces"]
    B --> C["Calculate Initial Momenta: $$\vec{p}_1 = m_1 \vec{v}_1, \quad \vec{p}_2 = m_2 \vec{v}_2$$"]
    C --> D["Determine Collision Type"]
    D --> E1["Elastic Collision"]
    D --> E2["Inelastic Collision"]
    E1 --> F1["Apply Conservation of Momentum: $$m_1 \vec{v}_{1i} + m_2 \vec{v}_{2i} = m_1 \vec{v}_{1f} + m_2 \vec{v}_{2f}$$"]
    F1 --> G1["Apply Conservation of Kinetic Energy: $$\frac{1}{2} m_1 v_{1i}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 v_{2i}^2 = \frac{1}{2} m_1 v_{1f}^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 v_{2f}^2$$"]
    G1 --> H["Solve for Final Velocities"]
    E2 --> F2["Apply Conservation of Momentum Only"]
    F2 --> G2["Use $$\vec{v}_{1f} = \vec{v}_{2f}$$ if perfectly inelastic"]
    G2 --> H
    H --> I["Analyze Results: velocities, kinetic energy change, impulse"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| Formula / Law                     | Meaning / Use                                                                                  |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| $$\vec{p} = m \vec{v}$$          | **Linear momentum** of an object                                                             |
| $$\vec{J} = \vec{F} \Delta t$$   | **Impulse**: force applied over time                                                         |
| $$\vec{J} = \Delta \vec{p} = m \vec{v}_f - m \vec{v}_i$$ | **Impulse-momentum theorem** relates impulse to momentum change                               |
| $$\sum \vec{p}_{initial} = \sum \vec{p}_{final}$$ | **Conservation of linear momentum** in isolated systems                                      |
| $$K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$        | Kinetic energy formula                                                                         |
| Elastic collision conditions:    | Both momentum and kinetic energy conserved                                                   |
| Inelastic collision conditions:  | Momentum conserved, kinetic energy decreases (energy lost to deformation, heat, sound)       |
| Perfectly inelastic collision:   | Objects stick together after collision, $$\vec{v}_{1f} = \vec{v}_{2f} = \vec{v}_f$$          |

## Connections & Comparisons

| Aspect                      | Elastic Collision                               | Inelastic Collision                            | Perfectly Inelastic Collision                     |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **Momentum**                | Conserved                                       | Conserved                                       | Conserved                                         |
| **Kinetic Energy**          | Conserved                                       | Not conserved                                  | Not conserved                                    |
| **Final Velocities**        | Different velocities for objects after collision | Different velocities, but less kinetic energy | Objects move together with common velocity       |
| **Energy Transformation**  | No loss; energy remains kinetic                 | Some kinetic energy converted to other forms  | Maximum kinetic energy lost within collision     |
| **AP Exam Focus**           | Requires solving simultaneous equations        | Focus on momentum only                          | Simplified momentum conservation with combined mass |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **impulse** with force alone; impulse depends on both force and time interval.
- Forgetting that **momentum is a vector**; directions matter in collisions.
- Assuming **kinetic energy is always conserved**; only true in elastic collisions.
- Mixing up **internal vs. external forces** when deciding if momentum is conserved.
- Neglecting to apply **impulse-momentum theorem** when forces act over time intervals.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define **linear momentum** and calculate it for single objects.
- [ ] Explain and apply the **impulse-momentum theorem** to relate force, time, and momentum change.
- [ ] Identify when **momentum is conserved** and apply conservation to collision problems.
- [ ] Distinguish between **elastic** and **inelastic collisions**, including kinetic energy considerations.
- [ ] Solve problems involving **perfectly inelastic collisions** where objects stick together.
- [ ] Analyze collisions in one dimension, accounting for vector directions.
- [ ] Recognize the role of **external forces** in system momentum changes.
- [ ] Use **kinetic energy calculations** to assess energy conservation or loss in collisions.

# Unit 5: Torque and Rotational Dynamics

## Overview
This unit explores **torque**, the rotational analogue of force, and how it causes objects to rotate. You will learn about **rotational inertia**, Newton’s second law applied to rotation, and the conditions for **static equilibrium** of rigid bodies. Mastery of these concepts is essential for solving AP Physics 1 problems involving rotational motion and equilibrium.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**               | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                         |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Torque ($\tau$)**       | A measure of the tendency of a force to cause rotation about an axis.          | Central to solving rotational dynamics problems on the exam.         |
| **Lever arm ($r_\perp$)** | The perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force. | Determines the effectiveness of a force in producing torque.        |
| **Rotational inertia ($I$)** | The resistance of an object to changes in its rotational motion, depends on mass distribution. | Key to applying Newton’s 2nd law for rotation; varies by shape.      |
| **Newton’s Second Law for Rotation** | $\sum \tau = I \alpha$, relates net torque to angular acceleration.          | Fundamental equation for analyzing rotational motion problems.       |
| **Angular acceleration ($\alpha$)** | The rate of change of angular velocity.                                       | Connects torque and rotational inertia; appears in many AP problems. |
| **Static Equilibrium**    | Condition where net force and net torque on a rigid body are zero.             | Essential for solving balance and stability problems on the exam.    |
| **Center of Mass (COM)**  | The point where the mass of a body can be considered concentrated.              | Used to analyze torque and equilibrium in irregular objects.         |
| **Rotational Kinetic Energy** | Energy due to rotational motion, $K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$.                  | Appears in energy conservation problems involving rotation.          |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Apply a Force ($\vec{F}$) at a Point"] --> B["Determine Lever Arm ($r_\perp$)"]
    B --> C["Calculate Torque: $\tau = r_\perp F$"]
    C --> D["Sum All Torques: $\sum \tau$"]
    D --> E["Use Newton's 2nd Law for Rotation: $\sum \tau = I \alpha$"]
    E --> F["Solve for Angular Acceleration ($\alpha$)"]
    F --> G["Analyze Rotational Motion or Equilibrium"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Formula / Law**                          | **Meaning / Use**                                     |
|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| $$\tau = r_\perp F = r F \sin \theta$$   | Torque from force $F$ applied at distance $r$ with angle $\theta$ to lever arm. |
| $$\sum \tau = I \alpha$$                   | Newton’s 2nd law for rotation: net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. |
| $$I = \sum m_i r_i^2$$                     | Moment of inertia for discrete masses; integral form for continuous bodies. |
| $$\alpha = \frac{d\omega}{dt}$$            | Angular acceleration as time derivative of angular velocity. |
| $$K_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$ | Rotational kinetic energy of a rotating object. |
| Conditions for static equilibrium:         | $$\sum \vec{F} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum \tau = 0$$ |
| $$\tau_{\text{net}} = 0 \implies \text{no angular acceleration}$$ | Static or rotational equilibrium condition. |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept**               | **Force**                         | **Torque**                         | **Linear Motion**                 | **Rotational Motion**               |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------|----------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Analogue**             | Force ($\vec{F}$)                | Torque ($\tau$)                  | Mass ($m$)                      | Moment of Inertia ($I$)            |
| **Effect**               | Causes linear acceleration ($a$) | Causes angular acceleration ($\alpha$) | $F = m a$                      | $\sum \tau = I \alpha$             |
| **Quantity**             | Vector                          | Pseudovector (depends on axis)  | Scalar                         | Scalar                            |
| **Resistance to change** | Mass                           | Rotational inertia               | Inertia in linear motion        | Inertia in rotational motion       |
| **Energy**               | Kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ | Rotational kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$ | Linear displacement ($x$)       | Angular displacement ($\theta$)    |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **torque** ($\tau$) with force ($F$); torque depends on both force magnitude and lever arm.
- Forgetting to use the **perpendicular component** of the lever arm or force when calculating torque.
- Mixing up **rotational inertia** ($I$) formulas for different shapes; always check the shape and axis.
- Neglecting to check **sign conventions** for torque (clockwise vs. counterclockwise).
- Assuming static equilibrium means zero force only; must also have **zero net torque**.
- Overlooking that **angular acceleration** is zero in equilibrium, not necessarily angular velocity.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define and calculate **torque** using force and lever arm.
- [ ] Explain the physical meaning of **rotational inertia** and how it depends on mass distribution.
- [ ] Apply **Newton’s second law for rotation**: $\sum \tau = I \alpha$.
- [ ] Determine conditions for **static equilibrium**: net force and net torque zero.
- [ ] Calculate **rotational kinetic energy** for rotating objects.
- [ ] Analyze problems involving combined **translational and rotational motion**.
- [ ] Use correct **sign conventions** for torque directions.
- [ ] Identify and compute the **center of mass** for torque calculations.

---

This guide prepares you to tackle rotational dynamics problems confidently on the AP Physics 1 exam by focusing on the essential concepts, formulas, and problem-solving strategies.

# Unit 6: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems

## Overview
This unit explores the dynamics of rotating objects, focusing on **rotational kinetic energy**, **angular momentum**, and the **conservation laws** that govern them. Understanding these concepts is crucial for solving AP Physics 1 problems involving rotating rigid bodies, where linear analogies extend to rotational motion.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**               | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                           |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Rotational Kinetic Energy** | Energy due to an object's rotation, analogous to linear kinetic energy.       | Essential for calculating energy in rotating systems and solving work-energy problems. |
| **Moment of Inertia ($$I$$)** | Measure of an object's resistance to angular acceleration, depends on mass distribution. | Determines how torque affects angular acceleration; critical for rotational dynamics. |
| **Angular Momentum ($$\vec{L}$$)** | Rotational analog of linear momentum, $$\vec{L} = I \vec{\omega}$$.           | Conserved quantity in isolated systems; key to solving collision and rotational motion problems. |
| **Torque ($$\tau$$)**          | Rotational equivalent of force, causes changes in angular momentum.           | Connects forces to rotational acceleration; used in Newton’s second law for rotation. |
| **Conservation of Angular Momentum** | Total angular momentum remains constant if no external torque acts.          | Fundamental principle for analyzing isolated rotating systems and collisions. |
| **Parallel Axis Theorem**      | Allows calculation of moment of inertia about any axis parallel to one through the center of mass. | Simplifies moment of inertia calculations for complex objects. |
| **Rotational Work and Power**  | Work done by torque and power delivered in rotational motion.                  | Links rotational motion to energy transfer; useful for mechanical energy problems. |
| **Rolling Motion**             | Combination of rotational and translational motion without slipping.           | Common in AP problems involving wheels and spheres; requires combining linear and angular quantities. |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Apply Torque ($$\tau$$)"] --> B["Angular Acceleration ($$\alpha = \frac{\tau}{I}$$)"]
    B --> C["Change in Angular Velocity ($$\omega$$)"]
    C --> D["Change in Angular Momentum ($$\Delta \vec{L} = I \Delta \omega$$)"]
    D --> E["Rotational Kinetic Energy ($$K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$)"]
    E --> F["Work Done by Torque ($$W = \tau \theta$$)"]
    F --> G["Power ($$P = \tau \omega$$)"]
```

This flowchart summarizes the cause-effect relationships in rotational dynamics: applying torque produces angular acceleration, changing angular velocity and momentum, which affects kinetic energy, work, and power.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| **Quantity**                     | **Formula / Definition**                                                                                     |
|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Rotational Kinetic Energy**   | $$K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$                                                                               |
| **Moment of Inertia**            | $$I = \sum m_i r_i^2$$ (discrete), or $$I = \int r^2 dm$$ (continuous)                                       |
| **Torque**                      | $$\tau = r F \sin \theta$$ or $$\tau = I \alpha$$                                                            |
| **Angular Momentum**             | $$\vec{L} = I \vec{\omega}$$                                                                                  |
| **Newton’s 2nd Law for Rotation**| $$\sum \tau = I \alpha$$                                                                                       |
| **Conservation of Angular Momentum** | $$L_{\text{initial}} = L_{\text{final}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad I_i \omega_i = I_f \omega_f$$               |
| **Parallel Axis Theorem**        | $$I = I_{\text{CM}} + M d^2$$ where $$d$$ is distance between axes                                            |
| **Work done by Torque**          | $$W = \tau \theta$$ where $$\theta$$ is angular displacement in radians                                       |
| **Power in Rotational Motion**   | $$P = \tau \omega$$                                                                                             |
| **Rolling without slipping**     | $$v = \omega r$$                                                                                                |

## Connections & Comparisons

| **Concept**                  | **Rotational Version**                          | **Linear Version**                          | **Key Difference / Connection**                        |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| **Kinetic Energy**           | $$K = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$                  | $$K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$                   | Moment of inertia $$I$$ replaces mass $$m$$; angular velocity $$\omega$$ replaces linear velocity $$v$$ |
| **Momentum**                 | $$\vec{L} = I \vec{\omega}$$                     | $$\vec{p} = m \vec{v}$$                      | Angular momentum depends on distribution of mass (via $$I$$) |
| **Force vs Torque**          | $$\tau = r F \sin \theta$$                       | $$F = m a$$                                  | Torque is force applied at a distance; causes angular acceleration |
| **Newton’s 2nd Law**         | $$\sum \tau = I \alpha$$                         | $$\sum F = m a$$                             | Both relate cause (force/torque) to acceleration (linear/angular) |
| **Conservation Laws**        | $$L_{\text{initial}} = L_{\text{final}}$$       | $$p_{\text{initial}} = p_{\text{final}}$$   | Angular momentum conserved when no external torque; linear momentum conserved when no external force |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **moment of inertia** with mass; moment of inertia depends on both mass and how it is distributed relative to the axis.
- Forgetting to convert angles to **radians** when using $$W = \tau \theta$$ or angular kinematics.
- Applying conservation of angular momentum incorrectly when **external torques** are present.
- Mixing up **rolling without slipping** conditions; must use $$v = \omega r$$ to relate linear and angular velocities.
- Neglecting the **parallel axis theorem** when the axis of rotation is not through the center of mass.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Explain the physical meaning of **rotational kinetic energy** and calculate it for rigid bodies.
- [ ] Calculate **moment of inertia** for common shapes and apply the **parallel axis theorem**.
- [ ] Use **torque** and **Newton’s second law for rotation** to find angular acceleration.
- [ ] Apply **conservation of angular momentum** to solve problems involving isolated rotating systems.
- [ ] Relate **work** and **power** in rotational motion using torque and angular displacement/velocity.
- [ ] Analyze **rolling motion** combining translational and rotational kinematics.
- [ ] Distinguish when to use linear vs. rotational analogs in problem-solving.
- [ ] Avoid common pitfalls related to units, external torques, and slipping conditions.

# Unit 7: Oscillations

## Overview
This unit explores **simple harmonic motion (SHM)**, focusing on oscillations of springs and pendulums. Understanding the **period**, **frequency**, and **energy transformations** in oscillating systems is essential for solving AP Physics 1 problems involving waves, forces, and energy conservation.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**                 | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                          |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) | Periodic motion where restoring force is proportional to displacement          | Foundation for analyzing oscillations and wave phenomena             |
| Period ($$T$$)              | Time for one complete oscillation                                              | Used to calculate frequency and relate to energy and forces          |
| Frequency ($$f$$)           | Number of oscillations per second                                              | Connects time domain to wave behavior; $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$            |
| Hooke’s Law                 | Restoring force in springs: $$F = -kx$$                                       | Governs spring oscillations; critical for force and energy problems  |
| Mass-Spring System          | Oscillator where mass attached to spring exhibits SHM                         | Model system for many AP problems; period depends on mass and spring constant |
| Simple Pendulum             | Mass swinging on a string under gravity exhibiting SHM                        | Tests understanding of gravitational effects on oscillations        |
| Energy in Oscillations      | Exchange between kinetic and potential energy during oscillation              | Key for conservation of energy problems and understanding motion     |
| Angular Frequency ($$\omega$$) | Rate of oscillation in radians per second: $$\omega = 2\pi f$$                 | Links time-based and angular descriptions of oscillations            |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Displacement from equilibrium (x)"] --> B["Restoring force (F = -kx for springs)"]
    B --> C["Acceleration towards equilibrium"]
    C --> D["Velocity changes direction at maximum displacement"]
    D --> E["Kinetic energy maximizes at equilibrium (x=0)"]
    E --> F["Potential energy maximizes at max displacement"]
    F --> A
```

**Explanation:**  
- The restoring force acts opposite displacement, causing acceleration toward equilibrium.  
- Velocity is zero at maximum displacement and maximum at equilibrium.  
- Energy oscillates between kinetic and potential forms, maintaining total mechanical energy.

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| Formula / Law                         | Meaning / Use                                           |
|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| $$F = -kx$$                         | Hooke’s Law: restoring force in a spring              |
| $$a = -\frac{k}{m}x$$               | Acceleration in SHM proportional to displacement       |
| $$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$    | Period of mass-spring system                            |
| $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$                 | Frequency, reciprocal of period                         |
| $$\omega = 2\pi f = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$ | Angular frequency of mass-spring oscillator            |
| $$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$    | Period of simple pendulum (small angles)                |
| $$E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$$    | Total mechanical energy in SHM (constant)               |
| $$K = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$             | Kinetic energy during oscillation                        |
| $$U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2$$             | Potential energy stored in spring                        |

## Connections & Comparisons

| Aspect                  | Mass-Spring System                                | Simple Pendulum                                  |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Restoring Force         | $$F = -kx$$ (spring force)                       | $$F = -mg \sin \theta \approx -mg \theta$$ (gravity) |
| Period Formula          | $$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}$$                  | $$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$                  |
| Dependence on Amplitude | Period independent of amplitude (ideal SHM)      | Period independent of amplitude (small angles)  |
| Energy Storage          | Elastic potential energy in spring                | Gravitational potential energy                    |
| Angular Frequency       | $$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}$$                   | $$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{L}}$$                   |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **period** and **frequency**; remember $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$, not equal values.  
- Using the pendulum period formula for large angles; it only applies for **small-angle approximations**.  
- Forgetting the negative sign in Hooke’s Law, which indicates the restoring force direction.  
- Mixing up energy forms: kinetic energy is max at equilibrium, potential energy max at max displacement.  
- Assuming damping or frictionless conditions without being told; most AP problems assume ideal SHM.  

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define **simple harmonic motion** and identify examples.  
- [ ] Calculate **period** and **frequency** for mass-spring and pendulum systems.  
- [ ] Apply **Hooke’s Law** to find restoring forces and accelerations.  
- [ ] Derive and use formulas for **angular frequency** $$\omega$$.  
- [ ] Analyze energy transformations between **kinetic** and **potential** energy during oscillations.  
- [ ] Explain the **small-angle approximation** for pendulum motion.  
- [ ] Solve problems involving total mechanical energy conservation in oscillating systems.  
- [ ] Distinguish between the characteristics of mass-spring systems and simple pendulums.

# Unit 8: Fluids

## Overview
This unit explores the behavior of fluids at rest and in motion, focusing on **density**, **pressure**, **buoyancy**, and **fluid flow**. Understanding these principles is crucial for solving AP Physics 1 problems involving liquids and gases, including applications of **Archimedes' principle**, **continuity equation**, and **Bernoulli's equation**.

## Key Concepts at a Glance

| **Concept**                | **What It Is**                                                                 | **Why It Matters (AP angle)**                                              |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Density** ($\rho$)      | Mass per unit volume of a substance: $\rho = \frac{m}{V}$                      | Determines how fluids exert pressure and whether objects float or sink.   |
| **Pressure** ($P$)        | Force per unit area exerted by a fluid: $P = \frac{F}{A}$                      | Fundamental for understanding fluid statics and dynamics problems.        |
| **Pascal’s Principle**    | Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout. | Basis for hydraulic systems and pressure calculations in fluids.          |
| **Archimedes' Principle** | Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid: $F_b = \rho_{fluid} g V$  | Explains flotation and buoyancy, key for solving related AP problems.      |
| **Buoyancy**              | Upward force exerted by a fluid opposing gravity on submerged objects.         | Determines if objects sink, float, or remain suspended in fluids.          |
| **Continuity Equation**   | $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$; fluid flow rate is constant in incompressible fluids.     | Used to analyze fluid flow speed changes in pipes and channels.            |
| **Bernoulli’s Equation**  | $P + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}$ along a streamline.   | Connects pressure, velocity, and height; essential for fluid dynamics.     |

## Core Processes / Relationships

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Density ($\\rho = \\frac{m}{V}$)"] --> B["Pressure ($P = \\frac{F}{A}$)"]
    B --> C["Pascal's Principle: Pressure transmitted equally"]
    C --> D["Hydraulic Systems: Force amplification"]
    B --> E["Archimedes' Principle"]
    E --> F["Buoyant Force ($F_b = \\rho_{fluid} g V$)"]
    F --> G["Object floats, sinks, or is suspended"]
    H["Fluid Flow"] --> I["Continuity Equation ($A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$)"]
    I --> J["Velocity changes with cross-sectional area"]
    J --> K["Bernoulli's Equation ($P + \\frac{1}{2} \\rho v^2 + \\rho g h = \\text{const}$)"]
    K --> L["Pressure-velocity-height relationship"]
```

## Essential Formulas / Laws / Rules

| Formula / Law                         | Description                                                                                   |
|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| $$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$              | **Density:** mass per unit volume                                                             |
| $$P = \frac{F}{A}$$                 | **Pressure:** force per unit area                                                             |
| $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$              | **Pressure in a fluid at depth:** $P_0$ is surface pressure, $h$ is depth                     |
| $$F_b = \rho_{fluid} g V_{displaced}$$ | **Buoyant force:** upward force on submerged object                                           |
| $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$               | **Continuity equation:** flow rate constant for incompressible fluids                          |
| $$P + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}$$ | **Bernoulli’s equation:** conservation of energy per unit volume along a streamline           |
| Pascal’s Principle                  | Pressure applied to enclosed fluid transmits undiminished throughout fluid                    |

## Connections & Comparisons

| Concept                 | Description                                      | Key Differences / Connections                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| **Pressure vs. Depth**  | Pressure increases with depth in a fluid        | $$P = P_0 + \rho g h$$ shows direct proportionality to depth |
| **Buoyancy vs. Weight** | Buoyant force opposes weight                     | Object floats if $$F_b \geq mg$$, sinks if $$F_b < mg$$       |
| **Continuity vs. Bernoulli** | Continuity relates area and velocity; Bernoulli relates pressure, velocity, height | Continuity ensures mass conservation; Bernoulli ensures energy conservation |
| **Static vs. Dynamic Fluids** | Static fluids exert pressure equally; dynamic fluids have velocity and pressure changes | Pascal’s principle applies to static fluids; Bernoulli applies to moving fluids |

## Common AP Exam Traps

- Confusing **pressure** with **force**; pressure depends on area, force does not.
- Forgetting that **density** is mass/volume, not just mass or volume alone.
- Misapplying **Bernoulli’s equation** between points not on the same streamline.
- Neglecting the effect of **fluid height** in pressure calculations.
- Assuming **buoyant force** acts only on fully submerged objects; it acts on any submerged volume.
- Using **continuity equation** for compressible fluids (like gases at high speeds) where it does not hold.

## Quick Review Checklist

- [ ] Define and calculate **density** and its role in fluids.
- [ ] Explain how **pressure** varies with depth and area.
- [ ] Apply **Pascal’s principle** to hydraulic systems.
- [ ] Calculate **buoyant force** using Archimedes' principle.
- [ ] Determine whether an object will **float, sink, or remain suspended**.
- [ ] Use the **continuity equation** to relate fluid speed and cross-sectional area.
- [ ] Apply **Bernoulli’s equation** to solve fluid flow problems.
- [ ] Distinguish between static and dynamic fluid scenarios on the AP exam.

flashcards.definition: A scalar quantity defined as mass per unit volume, expressed as $$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$ where $$m$$ is mass and $$V$$ is volume.
Force exerted perpendicular to a surface per unit area, mathematically given by $$P=\frac{F}{A}$$, usually measured in pascals (Pa).
Pressure exerted by a fluid at rest due to the weight of the fluid above, calculated by $$P=\rho gh$$ where $$\rho$$ is fluid density, $$g$$ acceleration due to gravity, and $$h$$ depth.
A principle stating that a change in pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid.
The pressure exerted by the weight of the atmosphere at a given point, approximately $$1.01 \times 10^5$$ Pa at sea level.

multipleChoice.questionText: Which of the following correctly expresses the pressure exerted by a fluid at depth $$h$$ in a container?
According to Pascal's principle, if the pressure on a confined fluid is increased at one point, what happens to the pressure throughout the fluid?
options: It increases only at the point of application.
It increases equally throughout the fluid.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: It increases equally throughout the fluid.

flashcards.definition: A law stating that a body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
The upward force exerted on an object submerged in a fluid, caused by differences in pressure acting on its surfaces.
An expression of conservation of mass for an incompressible fluid, $$A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$$, relating cross-sectional area and flow velocity at two points.
A principle relating fluid pressure, velocity, and elevation along a streamline: $$P + \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$$.
A type of fluid flow characterized by smooth, parallel layers of fluid with no disruption between the layers.
